pos: prep. phrase (toward us; in our direction)
etymology: From us and the Saxon directional ending -weard, toward — the same element in homeward, heavenward, outward. The Authorized Version preserves a construction English has since dropped. This suffix is not the noun ward (watch, custody, prison, as in Gen 40:4); the two words are unrelated, and the dictionary keeps a separate entry for that one.
biblical_def: Three times the Authorized Version turns a pronoun into a direction, and every one of them concerns something of God aimed at His people. His thoughts: “Many, O LORD my God, are thy wonderful works which thou hast done, and thy thoughts which are to us-ward: they cannot be reckoned up in order unto thee” (Psa 40:5) — not merely that God thinks, but that His thinking has a direction, and that direction is toward us, past counting. His power: “And what is the exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe, according to the working of his mighty power” (Eph 1:19) — and Paul immediately measures that power by the resurrection of Christ, so that the force aimed at believers is the same force that emptied the tomb. His longsuffering: “The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance” (2Pe 3:9). Thoughts, power, patience — all of them with a vector, and the vector points at the church. The archaic little suffix is doing real theological work, and modern English has no tidy way to say it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) notes that ward, from the Saxon weard, signifies direction or tendency toward, and is used in composition as in homeward, heavenward, and in the Scripture phrases us-ward and you-ward.
webster_full: WARD, a termination, Sax. weard, denotes direction or tendency to; as in homeward, heavenward, upward, downward.
It is from the root signifying to turn or incline.
His power to us-ward who believe. Eph. 1.
The thoughts which are to us-ward. Ps. 40.
The construction with a pronoun, as us-ward and you-ward, is now obsolete except in the Scriptures.
scriptures: 2 Peter 3:9
The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.
Ephesians 1:19
And what is the exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe, according to the working of his mighty power,
Psalm 40:5

Many, O LORD my God, are thy wonderful works which thou hast done, and thy thoughts which are to us-ward: they cannot be reckoned up in order unto thee: if I would declare and speak of them, they are more than can be numbered.
Ephesians 1:20
Which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places,
corruption_summary: 2 Peter 3:9 is detached from its us-ward and made a universal statement of divine intention, which is exactly the phrase the verse supplies to prevent it.
corruption_paragraphs: “Not willing that any should perish” is the most-quoted half-verse in the debate over the extent of the atonement, and it is almost always quoted with the first half of the sentence removed. Peter says God is longsuffering to us-ward — to a defined company, addressed throughout the epistle as those who have obtained like precious faith. The any and the all in the second half are governed by that phrase: He is not willing that any of them should perish, but that all of them should come to repentance, and the delay of the day of the Lord is explained as patience while the last of them are gathered. Read that way the verse is not a problem text for definite atonement; it is one of its clearest statements, and the archaic suffix is the hinge.

The dictionary is careful not to overcorrect. Scripture does present a genuine, sincere offer of the gospel to all who hear, and the impenitent perish by their own refusal; God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. What Reformed teaching denies is that God's saving purpose fails — that He wills the salvation of individuals who are nonetheless lost. Ephesians 1:19 is the answer in the same vocabulary: the power exerted to us-ward who believe is the power that raised Christ from the dead (Eph 1:20). A power of that order does not merely make salvation possible. It accomplishes what it was aimed at, and us-ward tells you where it was aimed.
roots_summary: Greek eis hemas (G1519), unto us, toward us; Hebrew elenu, toward us; Saxon weard, direction or tendency toward.
roots_lines: Greek eis hemas (G1519) — unto, toward us; 2 Peter 3:9, the phrase the Authorized Version renders to us-ward.
Greek makrothumei (G3114) — is longsuffering, long-tempered; patience with a term and a purpose.
Greek huperballon megethos tes dunameos (G5235, G3174, G1411) — the surpassing greatness of the power; Ephesians 1:19.
Greek energeian tou kratous tes ischuos (G1753) — the working of the might of His strength; the same verse, piling the words up.
Saxon weard — toward; Webster's root, and the reason English still has heavenward.
usage: “Longsuffering to us-ward” — and the any and all are governed by it.
“His power to us-ward who believe” — measured by the raising of Christ.
“Thy thoughts which are to us-ward” — more than can be numbered.

pos: prep. phrase (toward you; in your direction)
etymology: From you and the Saxon directional ending -weard, toward. The companion form to us-ward, and like it, preserved in English now only in the Authorized Version. This suffix is not the noun ward (watch, custody, prison, as in Gen 40:4); the two words are unrelated, and the dictionary keeps a separate entry for that one.
biblical_def: All three occurrences are Paul's, and all three are about the direction of a ministry. His conduct: “our rejoicing is this, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world, and more abundantly to you-ward” (2Co 1:12) — Paul lived plainly everywhere and most plainly toward the church that trusted him. His authority: “Since ye seek a proof of Christ speaking in me, which to you-ward is not weak, but is mighty in you” (2Co 13:3) — the Corinthians wanted evidence that Christ spoke through him, and Paul answers that the proof is aimed at them and already at work in them. And his commission: “If ye have heard of the dispensation of the grace of God which is given me to you-ward” (Eph 3:2) — the stewardship he received was not a general office but a grace given for them, the Gentiles. In each case the little suffix rules out a ministry that exists for itself. Conduct, authority, and calling are all described as pointed at particular people, and that is the New Testament pattern of office.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) notes that the termination ward, from Saxon weard, denotes direction toward, as in the Scripture phrases us-ward and you-ward, now obsolete in common speech.
webster_full: WARD, a termination [Sax. weard], denotes direction or tendency to; as in toward, forward, homeward.
The grace of God which is given me to you-ward. Eph. 3.
Which to you-ward is not weak, but is mighty in you. 2 Cor. 13.
The compound of a pronoun with this termination is peculiar to the older English and is retained in the common version of the Scriptures.
It answers to the Greek eis, unto or toward.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 1:12

For our rejoicing is this, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world, and more abundantly to you-ward.
Ephesians 3:2
If ye have heard of the dispensation of the grace of God which is given me to you-ward:
2 Corinthians 13:3
Since ye seek a proof of Christ speaking in me, which to you-ward is not weak, but is mighty in you.
1 Corinthians 9:2
If I be not an apostle unto others, yet doubtless I am to you: for the seal of mine apostleship are ye in the Lord.
corruption_summary: Ministry has been detached from a particular people, so that a man may have an audience and no flock, and influence with no one to answer to.
corruption_paragraphs: The whole force of you-ward is particularity. Paul's conduct, his authority, and his very commission are described as pointed at named congregations, and 1 Corinthians 9:2 makes the logic explicit: the seal of mine apostleship are ye in the Lord. The proof of his office was the existence of the people it had produced. The broadcast era has made the opposite arrangement normal — a teaching ministry with an enormous audience and no congregation, accountable to no elders, producing followers no one is responsible for. The dictionary does not condemn the wide dissemination of sound teaching; it notes that the New Testament never treats it as a substitute for a man being toward a particular people.

2 Corinthians 1:12 supplies the other half, which is the transparency that particularity requires. Paul says he behaved in simplicity and godly sincerity in the world and more abundantly toward them — the people who could actually check. A ministry aimed at a real congregation is one in which the members can see the man's ordinary life, his money, his household, and his temper. That is precisely why the qualifications for eldership in 1 Timothy 3 are almost entirely domestic and observable. Where no one is in a position to verify, the qualifications cannot be applied, and the office has quietly become something else.
roots_summary: Greek pros humas (G4314), toward you; eis humas (G1519), unto you; oikonomia (G3622), stewardship, dispensation; Saxon weard, toward.
roots_lines: Greek pros humas (G4314) — toward you, face-to-face with you; 2 Corinthians 1:12.
Greek eis humas (G1519) — unto you; Ephesians 3:2, of the grace given for them.
Greek oikonomia (G3622) — household management, stewardship; the dispensation of grace Paul received.
Greek dokime (G1382) — proof, tested evidence; 2 Corinthians 13:3, what the Corinthians demanded.
Greek sphragis (G4973) — a seal; 1 Corinthians 9:2, the congregation itself as the proof of the office.
usage: “More abundantly to you-ward” — plainest before the people who could check.
“The grace of God which is given me to you-ward” — a commission with an address on it.
“The seal of mine apostleship are ye in the Lord” — the people are the proof.

pos: n. (one who lends; one from whom a thing is borrowed)
etymology: From lend, Saxon laenan, from laen, a loan. In Scripture the lender is not a trade but a relation, and the relation is one of power.
biblical_def: Twice the Authorized Version names the lender, and both times to describe the power he holds. Solomon states it without any softening: “The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender” (Pro 22:7). The Hebrew for servant is the ordinary word for a slave, and the proverb is not moralizing about the lender's character — it is reporting a structure. Debt transfers authority. Isaiah then puts the pair into the great levelling of the day of the LORD: “as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the taker of usury, so with the giver of usury to him” (Isa 24:2) — priest and people, master and servant, creditor and debtor all alike when the earth is turned upside down. Against the structure Solomon describes, the law of Moses set an obligation that runs the other way: “thou shalt not harden thine heart, nor shut thine hand from thy poor brother: But thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him, and shalt surely lend him sufficient for his need, in that which he wanteth” (Deu 15:7-8). Lending to a poor brother is commanded, at no interest, with release at the seventh year — a loan designed from the start to end.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lender as one who lends; one from whom a thing is borrowed; and notes the borrower is servant to the lender.
webster_full: LEND'ER, n.
1. One who lends.
The borrower is servant to the lender. Prov. 22.
2. One who makes a trade of putting money to interest.
LEND, v.t. [Sax. laenan, from laen, a loan.] To grant to another for temporary use, on the express or implied condition that the thing shall be returned.
scriptures: Proverbs 22:7
The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender.
Deuteronomy 15:8
But thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him, and shalt surely lend him sufficient for his need, in that which he wanteth.
Deuteronomy 15:7

If there be among you a poor man of one of thy brethren within any of thy gates in thy land which the LORD thy God giveth thee, thou shalt not harden thine heart, nor shut thine hand from thy poor brother:
Isaiah 24:2

And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest; as with the servant, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller; as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the taker of usury, so with the giver of usury to him.
corruption_summary: Debt is now the ordinary condition of life and is marketed as freedom, while the law's command to lend to the poor brother is treated as impractical.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 22:7 is a sentence the modern economy is built on ignoring. Credit is presented as access, opportunity, and independence, and the relation it actually creates — the borrower is servant to the lender — is rarely named in the advertising. Scripture nowhere forbids borrowing, and it does not treat every loan as sin; but it insists that a man know what he has entered. A household in debt has transferred a portion of its freedom to someone else, and a church whose members are all in that position will find its members are not free to obey God in matters that cost money.

The other half is the part the church skips. Deuteronomy 15:7-8 does not merely permit lending to a poor brother; it commands it, forbids the hardened heart and the shut hand in the same breath, and requires the loan be sufficient for his need — with no interest charged to a brother and release in the seventh year. That is a loan designed to end rather than to compound. Nehemiah had to confront his own nobles for violating exactly this. The dictionary holds that lending at interest in ordinary commerce is lawful; what is forbidden is making a profit out of a brother's poverty, and what is commanded is an open hand toward it.
roots_summary: Hebrew lavah (H3867), to borrow or lend; malveh (H3867), the lender; eved (H5650), a servant or slave; neshekh (H5392), interest, literally a bite.
roots_lines: Hebrew malveh (H3867) — the lender; Proverbs 22:7 and Isaiah 24:2, the participle of lavah, to join or be joined by a loan.
Hebrew eved lo'ish malveh (H5650) — a slave to the man lending; the proverb uses the ordinary word for a bondservant.
Hebrew ha'avet ta'avitennu (H5670) — lending thou shalt lend him; Deuteronomy 15:8, the doubled verb of command.
Hebrew neshekh (H5392) — interest, literally a bite; the word for what may not be taken of a brother.
Saxon laenan, from laen — a loan; Webster's root.
usage: “The borrower is servant to the lender” — a structure reported, not a character judged.
“Thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him” — lending to the poor brother is commanded.
“As with the lender, so with the borrower” — and the day of the LORD levels both.

pos: n. (one who offends; a criminal; one who has broken a law)
etymology: Latin offendere, to strike against, from ob- and fendere, to strike. An offender is one who has struck against something — a law, a person, or a standard.
biblical_def: The two occurrences show the word used honestly and used as a weapon. Paul before Festus uses it with complete candour: “For if I be an offender, or have committed any thing worthy of death, I refuse not to die: but if there be none of these things whereof these accuse me, no man may deliver me unto them. I appeal unto Caesar” (Act 25:11). He does not plead exemption. If he is guilty he will die; if not, he may not be handed over — and he claims his legal right as a Roman. That is the Christian posture toward lawful authority: submission to the law and the use of the law's own protections, both without contradiction. The second is Isaiah's indictment of a corrupt court: woe to them “that make a man an offender for a word, and lay a snare for him that reproveth in the gate, and turn aside the just for a thing of nought” (Isa 29:21). Three techniques in one verse — criminalizing speech, trapping the man who reproves publicly, and defeating the just on a technicality. The man attacked is specifically the one who reproveth in the gate, that is, who speaks correction where the elders sat in judgment.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines offender as one that offends; one that violates any law, divine or human; a criminal; and one who does an injury.
webster_full: OFFEND'ER, n.
1. One that offends; one that violates any law, divine or human; a criminal.
Let no offender go unpunished.
2. One that does an injury.
The offender never pardons. If I be an offender, or have committed any thing worthy of death, I refuse not to die. Acts 25.
scriptures: Acts 25:11

For if I be an offender, or have committed any thing worthy of death, I refuse not to die: but if there be none of these things whereof these accuse me, no man may deliver me unto them. I appeal unto Caesar.
Isaiah 29:21
That make a man an offender for a word, and lay a snare for him that reproveth in the gate, and turn aside the just for a thing of nought.
Romans 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Acts 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
corruption_summary: Isaiah's method — making a man an offender for a word — has been rediscovered, and speech itself is increasingly treated as the offence.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 29:21 names a technique of corrupt power so precisely that it needs no updating: make a man an offender for a word, and lay a snare for him that reproveth in the gate. The gate was where the elders judged — the public square — and the target is the man who speaks correction there. Where a society begins to treat speech as the offence rather than as evidence about conduct, the first casualty is always public reproof, because reproof is the speech that costs someone something. The church has a direct stake in this: preaching is public reproof, and a settlement in which words are themselves actionable will reach the pulpit eventually.

Paul shows the Christian response, and it is neither defiance nor cringing. He submits to the court's jurisdiction, states plainly that he will die if he is guilty, denies the charge, and then uses his legal rights as a citizen to appeal to Caesar. Romans 13:1 grounds the submission — the powers that be are ordained of God — and Acts 5:29 marks the limit: we ought to obey God rather than men. Between those two verses is the whole Reformed doctrine of the magistrate: real authority, genuinely honoured, within a sphere that has a boundary, and a believer who uses every lawful protection without ever pretending he is above the law.
roots_summary: Greek adikeo (H91), to do wrong, to be a wrongdoer; Hebrew chata (H2398), to sin, to miss; machati'e adam bedavar, making a man an offender for a word; Latin offendere, to strike against.
roots_lines: Greek adiko (G91) — if I do wrong, am a wrongdoer; Acts 25:11, Paul's own conditional.
Hebrew machati'e adam bedavar (H2398, H1697) — making a man a sinner by a word; Isaiah 29:21.
Hebrew mokiach basha'ar (H3198, H8179) — the reprover in the gate; the public corrector, and the target.
Hebrew tohu (H8414) — emptiness, a thing of nought; the technicality by which the just is turned aside.
Latin ob- and fendere — to strike against; Webster's root.
usage: “If I be an offender… I refuse not to die” — no plea of exemption.
“I appeal unto Caesar” — and no contradiction between the two.
“Make a man an offender for a word” — the technique needs no updating.

pos: n. (one who wastes or squanders; and in Isaiah, a destroyer raised up by God)
etymology: From waste, Old French waster, from Latin vastare, to lay waste, from vastus, empty, desolate. A waster empties a thing — whether a purse or a nation.
biblical_def: Two occurrences, and the distance between them is instructive. Solomon puts the waster in the family of the sluggard: “He also that is slothful in his work is brother to him that is a great waster” (Pro 18:9). The point is that the two men arrive at the same emptiness by opposite routes — one spends what he has, the other never produces it — and a household ruined by neglect is as ruined as one ruined by extravagance. Isaiah uses the word of something far larger, and God is the one who made him: “Behold, I have created the smith that bloweth the coals in the fire, and that bringeth forth an instrument for his work; and I have created the waster to destroy” (Isa 54:16). This is the LORD telling Zion not to fear the weapons of her enemies, and the argument is startling: He made the man who forges the weapon and He made the destroyer who wields it. Both are creatures, both under orders. The verse concludes that no weapon formed against her shall prosper — not because weapons will not be formed, but because the smith and the waster alike are His.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines waster as one who wastes; one who is prodigal; a squanderer; and also that which destroys or lays waste.
webster_full: WA'STER, n.
1. One who wastes; one who is prodigal; one who squanders property; a spendthrift.
He that is slothful in his work is brother to him that is a great waster. Prov. 18.
2. That which wastes or destroys.
WASTE, v.t. [L. vasto, from vastus, waste, desolate.] To diminish by gradual dissipation; to squander; to destroy or lay waste.
scriptures: Proverbs 18:9
He also that is slothful in his work is brother to him that is a great waster.
Isaiah 54:16
Behold, I have created the smith that bloweth the coals in the fire, and that bringeth forth an instrument for his work; and I have created the waster to destroy.
Isaiah 54:17

No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper; and every tongue that shall rise against thee in judgment thou shalt condemn. This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD, and their righteousness is of me, saith the LORD.
Luke 16:1
And he said also unto his disciples, There was a certain rich man, which had a steward; and the same was accused unto him that he had wasted his goods.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 54:17 is claimed as a charm against all opposition, while the verse before it — which explains why it is true — is left out.
corruption_paragraphs: “No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper” is printed on more merchandise than almost any other line in Isaiah, and it is generally used as a personal talisman: whatever comes against me will fail. Verse 16 is the ground of the promise and it is almost never quoted with it. The reason no weapon prospers is not that God prevents weapons from being made — it is that He made the smith who makes them and the waster who uses them. That is a far harder and far better comfort. It does not promise the believer an untroubled life; it says that the destroyer himself is a creature under orders, and that the heritage of the servants of the LORD is secure because their righteousness is of Him, as the same verse ends.

Proverbs 18:9 has its own quiet application, and it belongs to stewardship rather than warfare. The slothful man is brother to the great waster — family, not merely similar. Scripture treats a man who neglects what he was given as of one house with the man who squanders it, which cuts against the common assumption that only active extravagance is culpable. The Lord's parable makes the same judgment of a steward accused that he had wasted his goods (Luk 16:1), and the servant who buried his talent was condemned for doing nothing at all with it. Emptiness is emptiness, however a man arrived.
roots_summary: Hebrew ba'al mashchith (H1167, H4889), a master of destruction; shachath (H7843), to ruin, destroy; Greek diaskorpizo (G1287), to scatter, waste; Latin vastare, to lay waste.
roots_lines: Hebrew ba'al mashchith (H1167, H4889) — a lord or master of destroying; Proverbs 18:9, rendered a great waster.
Hebrew mashchith lechabbel (H4889, H2254) — a destroyer to ruin; Isaiah 54:16, created by God for the purpose.
Hebrew charash (H2796) — the craftsman, the smith; the maker of the weapon, also created.
Greek diaskorpizon (G1287) — scattering, squandering; Luke 16:1, of the unjust steward's wasting.
Latin vastus, vastare — empty, to lay waste; Webster's root.
usage: “Brother to him that is a great waster” — neglect and extravagance are family.
“I have created the waster to destroy” — and that is why no weapon prospers.
“Their righteousness is of me, saith the LORD” — the heritage, and its source.

pos: n. (a clearing away; deliverance; the act of making an end of a thing)
etymology: From rid, to free or clear, from a Scandinavian root meaning to clear land. A clean riddance is a clearing that leaves nothing behind — and in Leviticus that is precisely what is forbidden.
biblical_def: The two occurrences use the word in opposite directions, and both are remarkable. The first is a prohibition attached to harvest: “And when ye reap the harvest of your land, thou shalt not make clean riddance of the corners of thy field when thou reapest, neither shalt thou gather any gleaning of thy harvest: thou shalt leave them unto the poor, and to the stranger” (Lev 23:22). Israel is forbidden to harvest efficiently. The corners stay uncut and the dropped stalks stay on the ground, not as charity dispensed but as a standing provision the poor come and gather with their own hands. Deuteronomy adds the forgotten sheaf, and gives the reason: “it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow: that the LORD thy God may bless thee in all the work of thine hands” (Deu 24:19). The second occurrence is a clearing that is made: in the day of the LORD's wrath “he shall make even a speedy riddance of all them that dwell in the land” (Zep 1:18). What the harvester may not do to his field, God will do to a guilty earth.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines riddance as deliverance; a setting free; and the act of clearing away or of disencumbering from something troublesome.
webster_full: RID'DANCE, n.
1. Deliverance; a setting free; as riddance from all adversity.
2. Disencumbrance.
3. The act of clearing away; as, to make a clean riddance.
Thou shalt not make clean riddance of the corners of thy field. Lev. 23.
RID, v.t. To free; to deliver; to clear; to disencumber.
scriptures: Leviticus 23:22

And when ye reap the harvest of your land, thou shalt not make clean riddance of the corners of thy field when thou reapest, neither shalt thou gather any gleaning of thy harvest: thou shalt leave them unto the poor, and to the stranger: I am the LORD your God.
Deuteronomy 24:19

When thou cuttest down thine harvest in thy field, and hast forgot a sheaf in the field, thou shalt not go again to fetch it: it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow: that the LORD thy God may bless thee in all the work of thine hands.
Zephaniah 1:18

Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them in the day of the LORD'S wrath; but the whole land shall be devoured by the fire of his jealousy: for he shall make even a speedy riddance of all them that dwell in the land.
Ruth 2:2
And Ruth the Moabitess said unto Naomi, Let me now go to the field, and glean ears of corn after him in whose sight I shall find grace. And she said unto her, Go, my daughter.
corruption_summary: Gleaning is claimed by every side of the welfare argument, and the law's actual shape — work required, dignity preserved, ownership intact — fits none of them neatly.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 23:22 is quoted as a proof text for state redistribution and dismissed as an ancient agricultural custom, and neither reading takes the law's shape seriously. The field remains the owner's; no official collects or allocates anything; and the poor do not receive a distribution — they go into the corners and reap for themselves. What is required of the owner is an efficiency he must forgo, permanently, as a term of holding land in God's country. What is required of the poor is labour. Ruth is the case study: a destitute Moabite widow who went to a field, worked all day, and was not shamed by it, and whose great-grandson was David. The arrangement preserves the dignity of both parties, which is precisely what the alternatives struggle to do.

Zephaniah 1:18 gives the word its other face and the church should not soften it. God will make a clean riddance of the impenitent in the day of His wrath, and neither silver nor gold shall deliver them. The two texts belong together. The same God who forbids a farmer to reap the last corner of his field, so that a stranger may eat, is the God who will clear a guilty land entirely. Mercy toward the poor and certainty of judgment are not competing dispositions in Him, and a theology that keeps one while discarding the other has not got the God of Leviticus or of Zephaniah.
roots_summary: Hebrew kalah (H3615), to complete, finish, make an end; pe'ah (H6285), the corner of a field; leqet (H3951), gleanings.
roots_lines: Hebrew lo tekhalleh (H3615) — thou shalt not finish, complete; Leviticus 23:22, the forbidden clean sweep.
Hebrew pe'ath sadkha (H6285) — the corner of thy field; the standing portion left uncut, and the name of a whole Mishnaic tractate.
Hebrew leqet (H3951) — gleanings, what falls in reaping; what Ruth gathered in Boaz's field.
Hebrew kalah nivhalah (H3615, H926) — a speedy, terrifying full end; Zephaniah 1:18, the same root turned on the guilty.
Scandinavian rydja — to clear land; the root behind English rid and Webster's riddance.
usage: “Thou shalt not make clean riddance of the corners of thy field” — efficiency forbidden by law.
“That the LORD thy God may bless thee in all the work of thine hands” — the forgotten sheaf stays forgotten.
“A speedy riddance of all them that dwell in the land” — the same word, and God is the reaper.

pos: n. pl. (conduct toward others; transactions; intercourse between parties)
etymology: From deal, Saxon daelan, to divide or distribute. To deal with a man is to divide something with him; one's dealings are the sum of those divisions, and therefore the visible record of a character.
biblical_def: Both occurrences concern a reputation that has travelled. Eli confronts his sons: “Why do ye such things? for I hear of your evil dealings by all this people” (1Sa 2:23). Note the source and the scope — the priest learns of his sons' conduct from all this people, which means everyone knew before the father acted, and his eventual rebuke was too mild and too late. The house of Eli fell over exactly this. The second is at Jacob's well: “How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans” (Joh 4:9). Here dealings is the ordinary word for social and commercial intercourse, and John inserts the note to explain why the woman is astonished. Christ crosses a barrier of centuries by asking for a drink of water. Set the two together and the word gives a working definition of integrity and its opposite: a man's dealings are what other people can report about him, and the Lord's first dealing with a Samaritan was to put Himself in her debt.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dealing as intercourse in buying and selling; traffic; conduct in relation to others; treatment; and intercourse of business or friendship.
webster_full: DE'ALING, n.
1. Intercourse in buying and selling; traffic.
2. Intercourse of business or friendship; concern.
The Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans. John 4.
3. Conduct in relation to others; treatment; as the dealings of a father with his children.
I hear of your evil dealings by all this people. 1 Sam. 2.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 2:23
And he said unto them, Why do ye such things? for I hear of your evil dealings by all this people.
John 4:9
Then saith the woman of Samaria unto him, How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans.
1 Samuel 2:29

Wherefore kick ye at my sacrifice and at mine offering, which I have commanded in my habitation; and honourest thy sons above me, to make yourselves fat with the chiefest of all the offerings of Israel my people?
John 4:10
Jesus answered and said unto her, If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water.
corruption_summary: Private character is treated as separable from public office, and the dealings a man is known for are reclassified as nobody's business.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Samuel 2:23 is a father's failure recorded in a single clause. Eli heard of his sons' evil dealings by all this people — the whole congregation knew what the priests were doing at the door of the tabernacle — and what he produced was a question and a mild remonstrance. The LORD's verdict is explicit, and it goes to the father's own appetite: honourest thy sons above me, to make yourselves fat with the chiefest of all the offerings of Israel my people (1Sa 2:29). Eli knew, Eli spoke, and Eli ate. He did not restrain them, and he was living off what they took. That is the standing indictment of every institution that investigates its own and issues a caution. Where a man's dealings are a matter of common knowledge and the authority over him produces only words, the authority is implicated.

John 4:9 shows the opposite corruption — a hardened boundary of no dealings at all, maintained for centuries by both sides, and crossed by Christ with a request for water. He does not begin by correcting her theology, though He gets there. He begins by needing something she has. That is the pattern for Christian dealing with those outside: not the careful avoidance that keeps a congregation unstained by keeping it unknown, and not an approval of what she was living in — He names it plainly a few verses later. He asks her for a drink and then offers her living water (Joh 4:10).
roots_summary: Hebrew ma'alal (H4611), a deed, a doing; Greek sunchraomai (G4798), to have dealings with, to use together; Saxon daelan, to divide.
roots_lines: Hebrew ma'alelekhem hara'im (H4611) — your evil doings; 1 Samuel 2:23, a word for deeds as they are reported.
Greek ou sunchrontai (G4798) — they do not use things in common, have no dealings; John 4:9.
Hebrew kihah bam (H3543) — he restrained them not, grew dim toward them; 1 Samuel 3:13, the failure named.
Greek hudor zon (G5204, G2198) — living water; John 4:10, what He offered after asking for a cup.
Saxon daelan — to divide, distribute; Webster's root, so dealings are what a man divides with others.
usage: “I hear of your evil dealings by all this people” — everyone knew first.
“Honourest thy sons above me” — the words were spoken; the restraint was not.
“The Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans” — and He asked her for a drink.

pos: adv. (in a manner agreeable to law; legitimately; according to the rules that govern a thing)
etymology: From lawful, from law, Saxon lagu, from lecgan, to lay — that which is laid down. To act lawfully is to act according to what has been laid down for that case.
biblical_def: Both occurrences are Paul's, to Timothy, and each concerns using something rightly rather than merely possessing it. The first is about the law itself: “But we know that the law is good, if a man use it lawfully” (1Ti 1:8). That is a remarkable sentence. The law is good — Paul will not concede an inch to those who blame it — and yet it can be used unlawfully, which is exactly what the teachers he is opposing were doing, wanting to be teachers of the law while understanding neither what they said nor what they affirmed. The law used lawfully convicts the lawless and drives men to Christ; used unlawfully it becomes a ladder, a speculation, or a weapon. The second is athletic: “And if a man also strive for masteries, yet is he not crowned, except he strive lawfully” (2Ti 2:5). A competitor who breaks the rules of the contest is not crowned however well he performs. Between them the two verses give the Reformed position on the law entire: the law is good, it has a proper use, it justifies no one, and the man who runs outside the rules receives nothing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lawfully as legally; in accordance with law; and lawful as agreeable or conformable to law; allowed by law; legitimate.
webster_full: LAW'FULLY, adv.
Legally; in accordance with law; without violating law.
We may lawfully do what the laws do not forbid.
LAW'FUL, a. Agreeable or conformable to law; allowed by law; legitimate; not contrary to law.
The law is good, if a man use it lawfully. 1 Tim. 1. Except he strive lawfully. 2 Tim. 2.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 1:8
But we know that the law is good, if a man use it lawfully;
2 Timothy 2:5
And if a man also strive for masteries, yet is he not crowned, except he strive lawfully.
1 Timothy 1:9

Knowing this, that the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and for sinners, for unholy and profane, for murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers, for manslayers,
Galatians 3:24
Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith.
corruption_summary: Both historic errors about the law — using it to justify and discarding it as abolished — are failures to use a good thing lawfully.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Timothy 1:8 is the verse that keeps the two ditches visible at once. Legalism uses the law unlawfully by making it a means of justification, which it was never given to be; Paul spends most of Galatians on that error and names the remedy in a figure — the law is a schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith (Gal 3:24). Antinomianism uses it unlawfully in the other direction, treating it as abolished for the believer and therefore irrelevant to his conduct. Paul answers that with the immediate context: the law is made for the lawless and disobedient, and his list in verse 9 is a straightforward exposition of the second table of the Decalogue. A law that still applies to murderers and liars has not been abolished.

2 Timothy 2:5 adds the note that the Reformed have always attached to the doctrine of perseverance, and it is not a threat but a description. An athlete who strives outside the rules is not crowned — his effort, energy, and sincerity count for nothing, because the contest had terms. This is the same point Christ makes about many who will say Lord, Lord. The gospel is free and it is not formless; salvation is by grace through faith in Christ alone, and that is itself the rule of the contest. A man running by some other route is running, but he is not in the race.
roots_summary: Greek nomimos (G3545), lawfully, according to rule; nomos (G3551), law; athleo (G118), to contend in the games; paidagogos (G3807), a schoolmaster.
roots_lines: Greek nomimos (G3545) — lawfully, agreeably to the rule; both 1 Timothy 1:8 and 2 Timothy 2:5, and nowhere else.
Greek nomos (G3551) — law; the noun Paul refuses to blame even while correcting its misuse.
Greek athle (G118) — to contend as an athlete; 2 Timothy 2:5, the games with their fixed terms.
Greek stephanoutai (G4737) — is crowned, with the victor's wreath; withheld from the rule-breaker.
Greek paidagogos (G3807) — the slave who conducted a child to school; Galatians 3:24, the law's lawful office.
usage: “The law is good, if a man use it lawfully” — good, and misusable.
“The law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless” — its lawful target.
“He is not crowned, except he strive lawfully” — the contest has terms.

pos: n. pl. (women held in bondage; female slaves or servants)
etymology: From bond, from Saxon bonda, a householder or villein bound to the soil, and women. The Authorized Version uses bondwoman and bondmaid for the female servant, and Paul makes the term the hinge of an allegory.
biblical_def: The plural appears three times and always in the context of a nation's ruin. Moses names it as the last stage of the covenant curses: “there ye shall be sold unto your enemies for bondmen and bondwomen, and no man shall buy you” (Deu 28:68) — a horror with a sting in the tail, offered for sale and not even wanted. It appears again in the Chronicler, where Judah's captives were to be kept as bondmen and bondwomen by their own brethren of Israel and the prophet Oded turned them back. And it appears in Nehemiah's great confrontation, where the enslavement is domestic: “lo, we bring into bondage our sons and our daughters to be servants, and some of our daughters are brought unto bondage already: neither is it in our power to redeem them; for other men have our lands and vineyards” (Neh 5:5). Jewish nobles were foreclosing on their own countrymen during the rebuilding of the wall. Paul takes the singular into his allegory of the two covenants — “Abraham had two sons, the one by a bondmaid, the other by a freewoman” (Gal 4:22) — and concludes, “we are not children of the bondwoman, but of the free” (Gal 4:31).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bondwoman or bondmaid as a woman slave, or one bound to service without wages, in distinction from a free woman.
webster_full: BOND'WOMAN, BOND'MAID, n. A woman slave, or one bound to service without wages, in distinction from a free woman.
Cast out this bondwoman and her son. Gal. 4.
BOND'MAN, n. A man slave, or one bound to service without wages.
In the feudal system, a villein; a tenant bound to services for his land.
There ye shall be sold for bondmen and bondwomen. Deut. 28.
scriptures: Nehemiah 5:5

Yet now our flesh is as the flesh of our brethren, our children as their children: and, lo, we bring into bondage our sons and our daughters to be servants, and some of our daughters are brought unto bondage already: neither is it in our power to redeem them; for other men have our lands and vineyards.
Deuteronomy 28:68

And the LORD shall bring thee into Egypt again with ships, by the way whereof I spake unto thee, Thou shalt see it no more again: and there ye shall be sold unto your enemies for bondmen and bondwomen, and no man shall buy you.
Galatians 4:22
For it is written, that Abraham had two sons, the one by a bondmaid, the other by a freewoman.
Galatians 4:31
So then, brethren, we are not children of the bondwoman, but of the free.
corruption_summary: Scripture's regulation of servitude is read as endorsement, while Nehemiah 5 — where a godly governor confronts his own class for it — is passed over.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard charge is that the Bible sanctions slavery because it regulates it, and the charge is answered from inside the text rather than around it. Nehemiah 5 is the case. The bondage there is not foreign conquest but foreclosure — Jewish nobles taking the sons and daughters of their poorer brethren for debt while the walls were going up — and Nehemiah's response is not a gradual reform. He is very angry, he calls a great assembly, he confronts the nobles publicly, he makes them swear restitution of the lands and vineyards, and he shakes out his lap as a curse on any who will not. The Mosaic law had built in release years, redemption rights, and a prohibition on ruling over a brother with rigour, precisely so that Nehemiah would have ground to stand on.

The New Testament carries the same trajectory further, and Philemon is its plainest instance: Onesimus is sent back as a brother beloved, and the whole letter makes his continued servitude morally impossible for a Christian master. Galatians 4 then turns the vocabulary into doctrine. The bondwoman and the freewoman are the two covenants, and the Christian is told what he is: not children of the bondwoman, but of the free. A faith whose central image of its own people is manumission has never been able to rest easy with chattel slavery, which is why the men who ended the British trade were reading these chapters.
roots_summary: Hebrew shiphchah (H8198), a maidservant; amah (H519), a female slave; Greek paidiske (G3814), a bondmaid; Saxon bonda, a householder bound to the soil.
roots_lines: Hebrew shephachoth (H8198) — maidservants, bondwomen; Deuteronomy 28:68, the end of the curses.
Hebrew kovshim (H3533) — bringing into subjection, treading down; Nehemiah 5:5, of brethren enslaving brethren.
Hebrew ga'al (H1350) — to redeem, act as kinsman-redeemer; what Nehemiah's poor said was not in their power.
Greek paidiske (G3814) — a bondmaid, servant girl; Galatians 4:22, of Hagar.
Greek eleuthera (G1658) — the free woman; Galatians 4:31, and the Christian's own standing.
usage: “We bring into bondage our sons and our daughters” — and Nehemiah called an assembly.
“Sold unto your enemies… and no man shall buy you” — the last of the curses.
“Not children of the bondwoman, but of the free” — the believer's standing.

pos: a. (born in the house or land; native; not foreign)
etymology: From home and born. The Authorized Version uses it for the native-born Israelite, set beside the stranger who sojourns — and in Jeremiah, for a slave born in the household.
biblical_def: The two occurrences use the word in its two senses. The first is one of the most consequential sentences in the Mosaic law, given at the Passover: “One law shall be to him that is homeborn, and unto the stranger that sojourneth among you” (Exo 12:49). One law. The native Israelite and the sojourning foreigner stand under the same statute, with the same protections and the same obligations, and Numbers repeats it: “One law and one manner shall be for you, and for the stranger that sojourneth with you” (Num 15:16). Leviticus makes it affection rather than mere policy: “the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt” (Lev 19:34) — and the reason given is memory. The second occurrence is Jeremiah's bitter question over a plundered nation: “Is Israel a servant? is he a homeborn slave? why is he spoiled?” (Jer 2:14). A homeborn slave was one born in the household, with no purchase price and no prospect of redemption, and the prophet asks whether Israel — a firstborn son — has somehow become that.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines homeborn as native; natural; and also domestic, not foreign.
webster_full: HOME'BORN, a.
1. Native; natural.
One law shall be to him that is homeborn. Ex. 12.
2. Domestic; not foreign.
A homeborn slave is one born in the house of his master, as distinguished from one bought with money.
scriptures: Exodus 12:49
One law shall be to him that is homeborn, and unto the stranger that sojourneth among you.
Leviticus 19:34
But the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God.
Jeremiah 2:14
Is Israel a servant? is he a homeborn slave? why is he spoiled?
Ephesians 2:19
Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God;
corruption_summary: One law is quoted for every immigration position on offer; what it actually establishes is equality before the law, which is narrower and sturdier than any of them.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 12:49 gets enlisted by all sides of the immigration argument, and it settles none of them. What the verse establishes is that the sojourner within Israel stood under the same statute as the native — the same protections and, equally, the same obligations. The stranger could eat the Passover, but he had to be circumcised first; he was covered by the sabbath rest and the gleaning laws, and he was also bound by the moral law and liable for the same offences. Equality before the law is what the verse gives, and it cuts against two errors at once: a xenophobia that denies the stranger the law's protection, and a sentimentality that exempts him from the law's claims.

Leviticus 19:34 then supplies the motive, and it is not policy but memory: thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt. A people that has been the foreigner is expected to remember what it felt like. The New Testament makes that memory the Christian's own: ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God (Eph 2:19). Every Gentile believer was once outside the commonwealth and is now homeborn by adoption, which is the strongest possible ground for how a church treats the outsider at its door. And Jeremiah 2:14 stands as the warning in the other direction: a son can live like a homeborn slave, and the prophet cannot understand why.
roots_summary: Hebrew ezrach (H249), a native, one springing from the soil; ger (H1616), a sojourner; yelid bayith (H3211), one born in the house.
roots_lines: Hebrew ezrach (H249) — a native, literally one that springs up as a tree from the soil; Exodus 12:49.
Hebrew ger (H1616) — the sojourner, resident alien; the party placed under the same law.
Hebrew torah achath (H8451, H259) — one law; the phrase of Exodus 12:49 and Numbers 15:16.
Hebrew yelid bayith (H3211) — born of the house; Jeremiah 2:14, a slave with no purchase price and no redemption.
Greek sumpolitai (G4847) — fellowcitizens; Ephesians 2:19, the Gentile made homeborn.
usage: “One law shall be to him that is homeborn, and unto the stranger” — same protections, same obligations.
“Thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers” — the motive is memory.
“Is he a homeborn slave? why is he spoiled?” — a son living like one born to bondage.
